findings.title: verify() ignores session expiry
findings.description: verify() returns a Session* whenever the token matches, never checking expires_at, so expired sessions remain valid indefinitely. Contradicts the documented contract that an expired token yields nullptr.

findings.title: require_admin() always rejects everyone
findings.description: Condition `role != "admin" || role != "owner"` is always true for any single role, so the function always returns false and no request can ever pass an admin check.

findings.title: bearer_token() uses a fixed 64-byte stack buffer and dereferences a possibly-null pointer
findings.description: strcpy into char[64] overflows on a long Authorization header, and when the header has no space, strchr returns nullptr and `space + 1` is undefined behavior, crashing the process on malformed input.

findings.title: Cache leaks every Entry* (destructor and erase paths)
findings.description: entries_ owns raw Entry* but the destructor only calls clear() and get()/set()/sweep() erase map nodes without deleting the pointed-to Entry, so cached entries leak for the lifetime of the cache.

findings.title: sweep() invalidates the iterator it is incrementing
findings.description: Calling entries_.erase(it) inside the for-loop and then ++it operates on a destroyed iterator (undefined behavior).

findings.title: set() is not LRU and leaks on overwrite
findings.description: Eviction picks entries_.begin() (map-key order) rather than the least-recently-used entry, and re-setting an existing code overwrites the pointer without deleting the old Entry. It also leaks when size >= limit with an existing key.

findings.title: utilization() always reports 0 until the cache is full
findings.description: Integer division `entries_.size() / limit_ * 100` is 0 whenever size < limit, so the dashboard reports 0% for any non-full cache.

findings.title: LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS treated as seconds despite being milliseconds
findings.description: The environment variable is documented and named as milliseconds, but the value is stored directly as Seconds, making the effective timeout 1000x too long (and LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS at line 29 has the same defect).

findings.title: LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT is parsed but never applied
findings.description: parsed is computed and immediately discarded with (void)parsed, so cfg.fetch_limit always keeps its default and the environment override has no effect.

findings.title: validate() always returns true
findings.description: Even when problems are collected and printed, the function returns true, so startup never fails on an invalid configuration, defeating the purpose of validation.

findings.title: format_row() returns a dangling pointer to a stack buffer
findings.description: row is a local char[128] destroyed when the function returns, so the returned const char* points at freed stack memory (undefined behavior on any use).

findings.title: write_snapshot() renames across filesystems and is not durable
findings.description: The temp file lives in /tmp while the destination is under dir; std::rename across filesystems fails. It also never fsyncs, so the claimed crash-safety guarantee does not hold.

findings.title: stats() divides by zero when the store is empty
findings.description: `g_store->total_hits() / g_store->size()` crashes with division by zero for an empty store, which is a normal startup state.

findings.title: report() mismatches the default report name
findings.description: export_csv() defaults an empty name to "links", but read_report() uses the raw (empty) name, so it reads `dir/.csv` which does not exist and returns an empty body.

findings.title: resolve() has an inverted expiry condition
findings.description: It erases and rejects links when `now < expires_at` (i.e. still valid) and serves them when expired, deleting live links on traffic and reviving dead codes — data loss in normal use.

findings.title: rename() validates `from` twice instead of validating `to`
findings.description: validate_code(to) is never called, so an invalid destination code can be inserted and corrupt the store; the documented validation of the new code is skipped.

findings.title: page() computes an out-of-bounds end iterator
findings.description: `end = all.size() + 1` exceeds the vector, and constructing the result from `all.begin() + offset` to `all.begin() + end` reads past the end (undefined behavior).

findings.title: success_rate() truncates to zero via integer division order
findings.description: `used / links_.size() * 100` is 0 unless every link has been used, so the reported percentage is almost always 0.

findings.title: remove() never restores the owner's quota
findings.description: quota_ is incremented on create but not decremented on remove, so a deleted link's slot is never freed, contrary to the documented behavior.

findings.title: top() returns the least-followed links instead of the most
findings.description: The comparator sorts ascending, then resize(n) keeps the first n (lowest hits). It also value-initializes extra Link entries when n exceeds the size.

findings.title: by_owner() matches owners by substring, not identity
findings.description: Uses owner.find(owner) != npos, returning links whose owner contains the query as a substring rather than links belonging exactly to that owner.

findings.title: extend() revives already-expired links
findings.description: It unconditionally sets expires_at = now + ttl, even for expired links, contradicting the documented rule that expiry is final.

findings.title: quotas() exposes a mutable reference to internal state
findings.description: Returns `std::map&` despite the documented snapshot contract that mutation must not affect the store, allowing callers to corrupt quota data.

findings.title: import_all() is not atomic
findings.description: Links are inserted one at a time, so a later validation failure leaves earlier inserts in place, violating the documented all-or-nothing semantics.

findings.title: prune() invalidates its iterator and returns the wrong count
findings.description: erase(it) followed by ++it is undefined behavior, and the function returns links_.size() instead of the number removed as documented.

findings.title: last_code() returns a dangling string_view
findings.description: It returns a string_view over the local `newest` string, which is destroyed at return; additionally it returns the lexicographically last key, not the most recently created link.

findings.title: Metrics::errors_ is uninitialized
findings.description: errors_ has no default member initializer, so Metrics::errors() reads an indeterminate value (used in stats()), unlike resolved_ and created_.

findings.title: warm_cache() spawns threads that are never joined
findings.description: The vector of std::thread is destroyed at return while threads may still be running, calling std::terminate. It also captures `link` by reference across the loop, dangling once the loop advances.

findings.title: check_targets() reads one past the end of links
findings.description: The loop condition `i <= links.size()` indexes links[links.size()], which is out of bounds (undefined behavior).

findings.title: janitor erases map entries while iterating
findings.description: store.all().erase(it) inside a range-for-style loop over the same map invalidates the iterator, causing undefined behavior on every sweep.

findings.title: Store's links_ and quota_ maps are shared across threads without synchronization
findings.description: Store has no mutex, but its mutable maps are touched by request handlers (create/resolve/rename/remove/import_all/extend) and by the janitor thread in worker.cpp, which iterates store.all() and erases entries. Concurrent std::map operations are a data race and can corrupt the tree or trigger use-after-free (e.g. janitor erasing a node while redirect() counts hits or create_link inserts).

findings.title: Cache entries_ and hits_ are accessed from multiple threads without synchronization
findings.description: Cache has no lock, yet get/set/erase/sweep and hits_ are reached from request threads, warm_cache worker threads, and the janitor thread's sweep(). Concurrent reads/writes on the std::map<Entry*> and the hits_ counter are a data race; combined with the janitor iterating and erasing entries, this can corrupt the cache or leave dangling Entry* values.

findings.title: Authenticator sessions_ is unprotected and verify() returns a pointer into it
findings.description: sessions_ is a std::map mutated by issue()/revoke() and read by verify() with no synchronization. verify() returns &pair.second, pointing into map storage; a concurrent revoke() erasing that node or an issue() rehashing/inserting can invalidate the pointer while a request handler still uses it, producing a data race and use-after-free. This also lets auth checks race.

findings.title: Metrics counters are non-atomic and errors_ is uninitialized
findings.description: resolved_ and created_ are plain long incremented from request threads (redirect, create_link) with no synchronization, so concurrent updates can be lost. errors_ is never initialized, so even a single read in stats() is undefined behavior before any write. Under load the dashboard counters drift.

findings.title: warm_cache spawns threads that are never joined and captures the loop variable by reference
findings.description: Each worker thread is pushed into a std::vector<std::thread> that is never joined; when warm_cache returns, the vector destructor calls std::terminate on every still-joinable thread, crashing the process. The lambda also captures &link, where link is the range-for reference; later-running threads observe a reused/dangling reference instead of the link they were supposed to warm.

findings.title: stop_janitor() does not join or delete the janitor thread
findings.description: stop_janitor() only flips g_running. The thread may still be sleeping for up to the interval and touching store/cache, so callers that destroy those objects first cause a use-after-free. g_janitor is also a raw pointer that is never deleted, leaking the thread object.

findings.title: Session tokens minted from std::rand()
findings.description: issue() builds the session token from two std::rand() values, which is a deterministic PRNG seeded with a low-entropy seed (often time). An attacker who can predict or brute-force the seed/state can forge a valid session token and take over another user's session. Tokens gate every write endpoint.

findings.title: verify() does not enforce session expiry
findings.description: verify() returns a session for any matching token without checking expires_at, even though the documentation says expired sessions are rejected. Stolen or leaked tokens remain valid forever, defeating the 12-hour lifetime and revocation-by-expiry.

findings.title: bearer_token() overflows a fixed 64-byte stack buffer
findings.description: std::strcpy(copy, header.c_str()) copies an unbounded attacker-controlled Authorization header into char copy[64]. A header longer than 63 bytes overflows the stack buffer, leading to memory corruption/RCE or at least a crash DoS.

findings.title: Session token written to stdout
findings.description: issue() logs the full bearer token to stdout (`auth: issued token ...`). Anyone with access to process logs (or log aggregation) can replay the token to authenticate as that owner.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback session secret
findings.description: When LINKD_SECRET is unset or empty, the authenticator silently falls back to "dev-secret-do-not-use". A deployment that forgets to set the env var ships with a publicly known secret used to sign/verify protected material.

findings.title: Password hashed with unsalted djb2
findings.description: hash_password() is a 32-bit djb2 accumulator with no salt and trivial work factor. Hashes are trivially brute-forced and collidable, and identical passwords share a hash. If these values are stored as passwords, offline cracking is cheap.

findings.title: secret_equals() short-circuits on length and bytes
findings.description: The comparison returns early on size mismatch and on the first differing byte, leaking prefix length/match information through timing. An attacker can recover a presented secret byte-by-byte.

findings.title: require_admin() can never return true
findings.description: The condition `role != "admin" || role != "owner"` is true for every possible role, so the function always returns false. Any code path that relies on this control can never grant admin access (fail-closed but non-functional authorization gate).

findings.title: CORS allows credentials with wildcard origin
findings.description: Every response sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. A cross-origin attacker site can issue credentialed requests to the API and read responses, defeating the same-origin protection on an authenticated API.

findings.title: Admin quota endpoint trusts spoofable x-admin header
findings.description: /admin/quotas grants access when the request carries `x-admin: true`, which any authenticated (or unauthenticated) client can set. This bypasses role-based authorization and exposes per-owner quota data to any caller.

findings.title: delete_link() has no ownership check
findings.description: An authenticated user can delete any link by code via DELETE /links, because remove() is called without comparing the link owner to the session owner. This enables unauthorized destruction of other users' links.

findings.title: create_link() lets caller impersonate any owner
findings.description: The owner is taken straight from req.query without binding it to the authenticated session. A user can create links attributed to another owner, polluting quotas and audit trails and bypassing per-owner limits.

findings.title: Open redirect in /out endpoint
findings.description: /out copies the attacker-controlled `next` query value verbatim into the Location header of a 301. This turns the service into an open redirector usable for phishing and credential-harvesting links.

findings.title: Report export path traversal and data exposure
findings.description: report() passes a user-controlled `name` to export_csv/read_report (path = dir/name.csv), allowing `../` traversal to read/write arbitrary files, and exports every owner's links regardless of the requester. Combined, any authenticated user can read arbitrary files and exfiltrate all links.

findings.title: Unknown token echoed in 401 response
findings.description: The 401 body includes the submitted token (`token <token>`), leaking credentials back (and to logs/proxies). An attacker probing tokens also gets them reflected, aiding credential theft.

findings.title: export_csv() path traversal via name
findings.description: path is built as `dir + "/" + report + ".csv"` with no confinement, so a name like `../../etc/passwd` escapes the export directory and overwrites/creates arbitrary files.

findings.title: archive_all() uses owner as filename (path traversal)
findings.description: Each owner's file is named `pair.first + ".csv"` without validation. A malicious/odd owner value (e.g. `../x`) writes outside dir, enabling path traversal and file overwrite.

findings.title: read_report() path traversal via name
findings.description: path = `dir + "/" + name + ".csv"` with no confinement, allowing an attacker to read arbitrary files by supplying a traversing `name`. Combined with /report, this is a file-read primitive.

findings.title: write_snapshot() uses a fixed world-writable temp path (TOCTOU)
findings.description: The snapshot is written to a fixed /tmp path then renamed into place. A local attacker can pre-create a symlink at that path, causing the service to overwrite an arbitrary file, or race the write (symlink swap) for a TOCTOU file-overwrite.

findings.title: resolve() inverted expiry check keeps expired links live
findings.description: resolve() erases the link when `Clock::now() < expires_at` (i.e. while still valid) and returns success otherwise. As a result expired links resolve and count hits, while valid ones are deleted — both an availability bug and a security control bypass (dead codes stay resolvable).

findings.title: extend() revives expired links
findings.description: extend() unconditionally sets a new expiry, ignoring the documented rule that an already-expired (dead) code must never come back to life. Attackers can re-arm expired links, bypassing intended link lifetimes.

findings.title: by_owner() substring match leaks other owners' links
findings.description: Owner matching uses `owner.find(owner) != npos` (substring), so querying owner "a" returns links owned by "alice", "admin", etc. Any caller listing by owner reads other users' links — an IDOR/information disclosure.

findings.title: quotas() returns mutable internal map reference
findings.description: Despite the comment that the map is a snapshot, quotas() returns a non-const reference to the internal quota_ map, allowing callers to mutate per-owner counts (inflate quotas, bypass limits).

findings.title: all() exposes internal link map for external mutation
findings.description: all() returns a mutable reference to the entire links_ map, bypassing Store invariants and letting any caller (e.g. janitor) mutate/delete links without validation or quota accounting.

findings.title: check_targets() reads one past end of links
findings.description: The loop bound is `i <= links.size()` (off-by-one), reading links[links.size()] out of bounds. Depending on layout this leaks adjacent memory into the returned string or crashes; reachable on the target-check path.
